document.title: Structured Knowledge Base for RAG-Based Diagnosis and Maintenance of Electric Motor Failures
document.application: Predictive and prescriptive maintenance using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)

scope.intended_use: Support CNN-to-RAG-to-LLM diagnostic pipelines by grounding generated reports in structured technical knowledge.

knowledge_schema.type: Fault class recognized by the diagnostic model
knowledge_schema.aliases: Alternative terms used in manuals, standards, and maintenance practice
knowledge_schema.description: Technical definition of the failure condition
knowledge_schema.physical_mechanism: Explanation of how the fault evolves physically/electrically
knowledge_schema.observable_evidence: Expected field evidence from thermal, electrical, mechanical, and operational inspection
knowledge_schema.system_effects: Consequences for performance, reliability, safety, and lifetime
knowledge_schema.maintenance_actions: Prescriptive actions recommended for maintenance teams

knowledge_schema.standards_and_guidelines: Normative or manufacturer references used for grounding
knowledge_schema.rag_retrieval_notes: Terms and reasoning cues that improve semantic retrieval

failures.description: Overheating represents an abnormal thermal condition in which the motor operates above its expected thermal behavior for the applied load, ambient condition, duty cycle, and cooling configuration. In induction motors, this condition is critical because temperature rise is directly associated with accelerated insulation aging, winding degradation, reduction of dielectric strength, and increased probability of premature failure.
failures.physical_mechanism: The fault is usually produced by an imbalance between heat generation and heat dissipation. Heat generation may increase due to overload, voltage imbalance, repeated starting, high current, winding defects, poor power quality, or mechanical friction. Heat dissipation may decrease due to obstructed ventilation, dirty cooling channels, damaged fans, high ambient temperature, or inappropriate installation clearance. When the thermal balance is lost, winding temperature increases and may propagate to bearings, frame, terminal box, and adjacent mechanical components.
root_causes: Operation above rated load or service factor
Restricted airflow or blocked ventilation ducts
Fan damage, fan obstruction, or ineffective cooling
Frequent start-stop cycles or excessive starting current
Voltage imbalance, undervoltage, overvoltage, or unstable supply
High ambient temperature or inadequate installation clearance
Winding insulation degradation or partial short-circuit
Mechanical friction caused by bearing degradation or misalignment

thermal: Localized hot spots near windings, terminal box, bearing housing, or cooling path
electrical: Thermal protection or overload relay tripping
mechanical: Abnormal bearing noise when overheating is caused by friction
Reduced speed or torque under load
operational: Smell of heated insulation in severe cases

system_effects: Reduced dielectric strength of winding insulation
Possible activation of thermal or overload protection devices
maintenance_actions: Compare operating current with nameplate values under the same load condition
Inspect ventilation paths, fan, air inlets, and external cooling surfaces
Clean dust, oil, and contaminants from the motor housing and cooling channels
Check load condition and verify whether the driven machine is overloaded or mechanically restricted
Measure phase voltages and currents to identify imbalance or abnormal supply conditions
Verify thermal protection settings and sensor operation
Inspect winding insulation condition when overheating is recurrent or severe
diagnostic_checks: Measure temperature trend under steady load
Compare current in all three phases
Inspect airflow direction and fan operation
Check insulation resistance if overheating persists after cleaning and load correction
Correlate thermal image with bearing and winding locations

standards_and_guidelines.relevance: Provides rating, performance, and temperature-rise principles for rotating electrical machines.
Used as a complementary Brazilian reference for induction motor performance and thermal behavior.
Supports the relationship between thermal stress, winding degradation, and common motor damage patterns.
Support inspection of ventilation, load, cleanliness, bearing condition, and operating environment.

reasoning_cues: If the CNN indicates overheating, retrieve entries that connect thermal rise to load, ventilation, power quality, and insulation degradation.

failures.description: A ventilation defect occurs when the motor cooling system cannot remove the heat generated during operation. This may be caused by fan failure, obstruction of air passages, dust accumulation, restricted installation clearance, or inappropriate cooling configuration. Although it often appears as overheating in thermographic images, its causal mechanism is specifically associated with ineffective heat dissipation.
failures.physical_mechanism: Induction motors depend on internal and/or external air circulation to transfer heat from windings, rotor, stator core, and housing to the surrounding environment. When air inlets, exhaust paths, cooling ribs, rotor ducts, or fans are blocked or degraded, heat accumulates even if the electrical load is within nominal limits. The resulting thermal pattern may show progressive heating around the frame and regions close to the cooling path.
root_causes: Dust or contamination blocking air intake/exhaust
Damaged, loose, or broken cooling fan
Incorrect motor installation with insufficient clearance
Obstructed cooling fins or external housing contamination
Foreign material inside ventilation channels
Operation in a high-temperature or poorly ventilated environment
Incorrect cooling method for the application

thermal: Temperature rise distributed over the frame
Hot regions near air outlet or blocked cooling path
Thermal gradient inconsistent with normal airflow
electrical: Current may remain near nominal when load is not the primary cause
Overload relay may trip after thermal accumulation
mechanical: Abnormal fan noise or absence of airflow
Contamination around fan cover or cooling ducts
operational: Motor heats faster than expected after cleaning/load changes

system_effects: Reduced bearing lubricant life due to elevated temperature
Increased risk of secondary overheating faults
maintenance_actions: Clean air inlets, exhaust openings, fan cover, cooling fins, and accessible ducts
Inspect fan integrity, fixation, direction, and rotation
Verify installation clearance around the motor
Remove dust, oil, and contaminants from the housing
Confirm whether the cooling method is compatible with the motor design and application
Monitor post-cleaning temperature trend to verify recovery
diagnostic_checks: Compare temperature before and after cleaning ventilation paths
Verify airflow with motor operating under safe conditions
Inspect fan cover and cooling ribs visually
Check whether thermal anomaly persists under reduced load
Distinguish ventilation defect from overload by combining thermal and current evidence

standards_and_guidelines.relevance: Defines cooling methods and classification for rotating electrical machines.
Support recommendations for keeping air passages clean and avoiding restricted ventilation.

reasoning_cues: When CNN predicts ventilation defect, prioritize documents that separate heat generation from heat dissipation and recommend cleaning/airflow verification.

failures.description: Phase loss is an electrical supply fault in which one phase of a three-phase motor supply is interrupted or becomes unavailable. The motor may continue operating under abnormal conditions, but current redistribution in the remaining phases produces imbalance, torque reduction, vibration, and rapid thermal stress.
failures.physical_mechanism: When one supply phase is lost, the rotating magnetic field becomes unbalanced. The remaining phases can draw excessive current while torque capability decreases. This condition increases copper losses, produces pulsating torque, raises winding temperature, and may lead to protective shutdown or winding damage if not interrupted quickly.
root_causes: Blown fuse or tripped breaker in one phase
Loose, oxidized, or broken terminal connection
Contactor pole failure or mechanical wear
Cable rupture or poor crimping
Protection device misadjustment
Power supply instability or upstream distribution fault

thermal: Asymmetric heating pattern in windings or terminal region
Temperature rise associated with current imbalance
operational: Motor hums, heats, trips, or fails to start under load

system_effects: Mechanical stress on rotor and coupling
Potential winding burnout under prolonged operation
maintenance_actions: Measure line-to-line voltages and phase currents
Inspect fuses, circuit breakers, contactors, terminals, and cable connections
Install or verify phase-failure and phase-sequence protection relays
Tighten terminals according to manufacturer recommendations
Investigate upstream power quality and distribution faults
Do not restart the motor until the missing phase cause is removed
diagnostic_checks: Confirm voltage presence in all phases
Compare current imbalance under no-load and loaded conditions
Inspect contactor contacts for wear or one-pole failure
Check thermal image for asymmetric heating
Verify protection relay operation

standards_and_guidelines.relevance: Provides safety requirements for electrical equipment of machines, including protective and control considerations.
Support inspection of terminals, supply conditions, and safe isolation before electrical maintenance.

reasoning_cues: Retrieve electrical-safety and current-imbalance content when the classifier indicates lack of phase.

failures.description: Blocked rotor is a severe condition in which the rotor or driven shaft cannot rotate freely because of mechanical obstruction, bearing seizure, load jamming, coupling misalignment, or internal interference. It is characterized by very high starting current, absence or reduction of rotation, and rapid thermal rise.
failures.physical_mechanism: During a locked-rotor event, the motor behaves similarly to a stalled electromagnetic system. Because rotation is prevented, back electromotive force is not properly established and the current remains high. The resulting Joule losses in stator windings can cause rapid overheating. Mechanical stress may also be transferred to bearings, shaft, coupling, and driven equipment.
root_causes: Bearing seizure or severe bearing degradation
Mechanical obstruction in the driven load
Coupling misalignment or coupling locking
Rotor-stator rubbing
Foreign object inside fan, shaft, or driven mechanism
Excessive load torque at startup
Incorrect assembly after maintenance

thermal: Rapid temperature increase shortly after energization
Localized heating near windings or bearing region depending on cause
electrical: Protection trip by thermal or magnetic device
Motor fails to reach rated speed
mechanical: Shaft does not rotate or rotates with difficulty
Abnormal noise, scraping, or sudden locking
High mechanical resistance when manually inspected after safe isolation
operational: Burning smell if energization is prolonged

system_effects: Damage to bearings, shaft, coupling, or driven load
Activation of magnetic or thermal protection
High safety risk during repeated starts
maintenance_actions: De-energize and lock out the equipment before mechanical inspection
Check whether shaft rotates freely by hand when safe and decoupled
Inspect bearings, coupling, fan, and driven machine for obstruction
Measure winding continuity and insulation resistance after severe event
Verify protection device coordination and trip history
Avoid repeated starting attempts until the mechanical cause is corrected
diagnostic_checks: Compare starting current with expected locked-rotor behavior
Inspect mechanical coupling and driven load
Check bearings for seizure or excessive friction
Verify whether rotor rub marks or foreign objects are present
Confirm that protection operated correctly

standards_and_guidelines.relevance: Provides motor rating/performance context relevant to abnormal starting and thermal limits.
Support safe inspection, bearing checks, coupling verification, and avoidance of repeated starts under abnormal mechanical conditions.

reasoning_cues: For blocked rotor, retrieve both electrical protection and mechanical obstruction content.

failures.description: Bearing failure is a mechanical degradation condition associated with wear, contamination, lubrication deficiency, misalignment, overloading, electrical discharge, or fatigue. In induction motors, bearing faults are critical because they increase friction, vibration, acoustic noise, and localized heat near the bearing housing, potentially leading to rotor misalignment and secondary electrical or thermal faults.
failures.physical_mechanism: Bearing degradation increases rolling or sliding friction and produces vibration signatures that evolve from incipient defects to severe mechanical damage. Poor lubrication or contamination accelerates surface wear and increases temperature. As bearing clearance or damage progresses, shaft alignment may deteriorate, causing rotor eccentricity, additional losses, and possible contact between rotating and stationary parts.
root_causes: Insufficient or degraded lubricant
Excessive lubrication causing heating or contamination retention
Ingress of dust, moisture, or chemical contaminants
Misalignment between motor and driven load
Excessive radial or axial load
Fatigue from long service life
Improper mounting or handling during maintenance
Electrical bearing currents in specific drive applications

thermal: Localized hot spot at drive-end or non-drive-end bearing housing
electrical: Current may increase slightly due to mechanical load/friction
Variable-frequency drive applications may show bearing-current related damage
operational: Progressive increase in noise and temperature
Potential shutdown due to vibration or thermal protection

system_effects: Increased vibration transmitted to the foundation
Possible rotor/stator contact in severe cases
maintenance_actions: Inspect bearing temperature, vibration, and acoustic behavior
Lubricate according to manufacturer interval, grease type, and quantity
Avoid overgreasing and contamination during lubrication
Inspect seals and shields against ingress of dust/moisture
Check alignment between motor and driven equipment
Replace worn bearings before catastrophic failure
Record bearing temperature and vibration trends after intervention
diagnostic_checks: Compare drive-end and non-drive-end bearing temperatures
Evaluate vibration severity and trend over time
Inspect lubricant condition and maintenance history
Check shaft/coupling alignment
Confirm whether heating remains after load and ventilation correction

standards_and_guidelines.relevance: Used for vibration severity evaluation of rotating machinery, depending on equipment class and current standard adoption.
Support bearing lubrication, replacement, inspection, and contamination prevention procedures.

reasoning_cues: For bearing failure, retrieve mechanical evidence, lubrication procedures, vibration interpretation, and thermal localization near bearing housing.

failures.description: Normal operation corresponds to a condition in which the motor operates within expected electrical, thermal, mechanical, and environmental limits. No abnormal heating pattern, excessive vibration, phase imbalance, or mechanical restriction is detected. This class is important as a baseline for comparison against fault conditions.
failures.physical_mechanism: In normal operation, heat generated by copper losses, iron losses, mechanical friction, and stray losses is balanced by the cooling system and the surrounding environment. Phase currents remain balanced, vibration and noise remain stable, and thermal distribution is compatible with motor construction, load, duty cycle, and cooling method.
root_causes: No failure mechanism detected
Operation within rated load and environmental limits
Adequate cooling and ventilation
Stable three-phase power supply
Acceptable bearing and lubrication condition

thermal: Thermal pattern compatible with load and cooling path
operational: No reduction in torque or speed

system_effects: Expected service life when preventive maintenance is maintained
maintenance_actions: Continue scheduled preventive maintenance
Monitor temperature, current, and vibration trends
Maintain ventilation cleanliness
Periodically tighten electrical connections following safe procedures
Lubricate bearings according to manufacturer recommendations
Use the normal pattern as baseline for anomaly detection
diagnostic_checks: Compare current operation with historical baseline
Confirm absence of thermal hotspots
Check phase-current balance
Verify routine maintenance records
Inspect for early deviations in trend data

standards_and_guidelines.relevance: Provides motor rating and performance context for nominal operation.
Support preventive inspection routines, cleaning, lubrication, and safe operation practices.

reasoning_cues: For normal class, retrieve baseline and preventive maintenance content rather than fault-correction procedures.

retrieval_configuration.recommended_chunking: Index each fault entry as one main document and optionally index subdocuments for physical mechanism, observable evidence, maintenance actions, and standards.
retrieval_configuration.recommended_top_k: 3 to 5 depending on knowledge base size; use reranking when expanding to manuals and standards.
retrieval_configuration.query_template: Fault: {predicted_class}; confidence: {confidence}; observed evidence: {thermal/electrical/mechanical evidence if available}; retrieve causes, symptoms, risks, actions, and standards.
retrieval_configuration.generation_instruction: Use only retrieved context. Distinguish observed evidence from inferred causes. Mention standards only as references/guidelines, not as direct quotations unless authorized.
